lines: Watch what actually breaks here. Nothing technical. The pipeline runs exactly the same way it always has.
What breaks is licensing. The endpoint it was built on was never supposed to be used this way, and that fact didn't exist until someone wrote it down.
Before the four mechanisms, notice what the hook is actually testing. Not whether the connector still runs — it does.
It's testing which specific combination of mechanism and use crossed a line SAP drew somewhere else entirely. Which one do you think it is?
answer: The operational data provisioning framework, used over R F C, by a tool outside SAP, moving data out.
That exact combination is what got restricted. The protocol itself, and most of the other mechanisms, were never touched.

lines: Look at what sits underneath that semantic view. Cryptic, application-built field names nobody designed for a human to read.
A C D S view is SAP's own answer to that — names and relationships added on top, so an extraction tool reads the view, not the raw mess beneath it.
Watch what each mechanism actually notices, not how fast it runs.
Three of these catch every insert, update and delete. One of them — the REST-based one — has a documented blind spot: it can quietly miss a delete entirely.
Follow this note through its own history, because the wording changed meaning each time.
Unsupported, then outright prohibited, then redirected toward SAP's own replacement platform. Three different statements, three different years, and the connector itself never moved.
Notice this isn't a side project. SAP built this with an outside partner, inside its own flagship platform.
Data moves both directions between the two environments, and a separate catalog governs who can see what on either side.
Watch what this query actually returns when the date is wrong, not just that it returns something.
It doesn't hand back an old version of the record. It hands back nothing at all — which looks exactly like the record never existed.
If you keep one thing: a mechanism's real limit is what it can see, not how fast it runs.
Views exist because raw tables weren't meant to be read directly. A support note's wording is a clock, not a warning you read once. And a wrong date doesn't return stale data — it returns none.
Before I answer, notice what this team's pipeline is actually doing: running the same as-of date every single night.
A brand-new record just started existing after that date. What does the query do with it?
answer: The new record falls outside that fixed date's effective window, so it's filtered out entirely.
Not a missed delete, and not a licensing problem — those are this topic's other two failure modes. This one is a stale date quietly hiding a record that already exists.
